question: Does the intervention cause the outcome?

steps.title: Enrol
steps.text: Screen people against the eligibility criteria. Those who fit and agree are enrolled; the rest are counted, not dropped from view.

quotes.text: a clear understanding of these criteria is one of several elements required to judge to whom the results of a trial apply

steps.title: Allocate by chance
steps.text: A random sequence, not a person, decides who gets the intervention, and nobody enrolling patients can see the next assignment.

quotes.text: With random allocation, each participant has a known probability of receiving each intervention before one is assigned, but the assigned intervention is determined by a chance process and cannot be predicted.
when properly implemented, it eliminates selection bias, balancing both known and unknown prognostic factors, in the assignment of treatments.
allocation concealment, a critical mechanism that prevents foreknowledge of treatment assignment

steps.title: Treat
steps.text: One arm gets the intervention, the other the control. Where possible the control looks the same, so nobody knows who got what.

quotes.text: The term “blinding” or “masking” refers to withholding information about the assigned interventions from people involved in the trial who may potentially be influenced by this knowledge.

steps.title: Follow up
steps.text: Follow both arms for the same time and measure the same outcome. Count everyone who drops out, and why.

quotes.text: it may be difficult for readers to discern whether and why some participants did not receive the treatment as allocated, were lost to follow-up, or were excluded from the analysis.
screening, enrolment, intervention allocation, follow-up, and assessment
quotes.where: Fig 5, the phases of the flow diagram

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Compare the outcome between the arms, analysing everyone in the arm they were allocated to. Because chance made the arms alike, the difference estimates the effect.

quotes.text: analyse all participants according to their original group assignment, regardless of what subsequently occurred

external-validity.text: External validity, also called generalisability or applicability, is the extent to which the results of a study can be generalised to other circumstances.

exercise.title: Why chance and not a doctor?
exercise.intro: Each dot is a patient. Some are severely ill (red), which nobody records. Let a doctor choose who gets the new treatment, or let chance choose, and see how many severe patients each arm starts with.

quote.text: Without randomisation, treatment comparisons may be prejudiced, whether consciously or not, by selection of participants of a particular kind to receive a particular treatment.

exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise.
exercise.doctor_rule: The simulated doctor gives the new treatment to the patients who look more likely to recover; severity shows only partly, so the doctor's impression is severity plus noise.
